title: F1 to race in Sao Paulo through to 2035 following new deal
excerpt:
Formula 1 will continue to race in Brazil through to 2035 following a five-year extension, securing the future of one of the sport’s most iconic and historic venues.

The Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace – otherwise known as Interlagos – has been part of the calendar for over 50 years and delivered plenty of memorable races, such as Max Verstappen’s 2024 charge from P17 to victory.

Combining an undulating layout with Brazil’s passion for motorsport, the track consistently produces exciting wheel-to-wheel racing in front of vibrant crowds, and has seen a total of six Drivers’ Championships be decided, including those won by current drivers Fernando Alonso and Lewis Hamilton.

The country’s fanbase has increased to 75.8 million – 44% of whom are female and 41% of whom are under 35 – whilst attendances at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix have also grown, reaching 303,627 in 2025, up from 291,717 the year before.

Furthermore, F1 delivers a significant economic impact in the local community and more widely, with the 2025 event providing R$2.3 billion for Sao Paulo – a 9.7% increase compared to the previous record in 2024.

The sport also entered into an agreement last year with Brazilian broadcaster Globo, giving paying subscribers to SporTV the option to watch every on-track session live and on-demand, with additional live free-to-air coverage of 15 Grands Prix available throughout the season.

As part of the new five-year extension, the office of the Mayor of Sao Paulo, Ricardo Nunes, will continue to make significant investments to deliver a world-class spectacle, further enhancing the experience for fans and guests in the years ahead.

Stefano Domenicali, President and CEO of Formula 1, said: “Brazil is an important part of Formula 1’s history and our future, and I am delighted that this five-year extension will see us continue racing in Sao Paulo until 2035.

“The passion of our Brazilian fans is extraordinary, and every time we return to Interlagos we feel their energy in the grandstands and in the city of Sao Paulo.

Everything you need to know about the Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace

“Brazil has produced an incredible 33 Formula 1 drivers, including Gabriel Bortoleto and Rafael Camara who are racing this weekend in front of their home crowd, which will add to the many previous unforgettable racing moments in Sao Paulo.

“The continued success and excitement surrounding the event shows why it holds such a special place on our calendar, and this agreement underlines our long-term commitment to Brazil.

“I would like to thank the Mayor of Sao Paulo, Nunes, and the President and CEO of Sao Paulo Grand Prix, Alan Adler, for their continued commitment and investment. Together, we will build on this success and make the experience even better for our fans in the years ahead.”

Nunes, Mayor of Sao Paulo, said: “The renewal of the Formula 1 contract for a further five years is a very significant achievement for Sao Paulo.

“We are ensuring the continuity of one of the world’s biggest sporting events, which boosts the economy, creates jobs, strengthens tourism and raises our city’s international profile.

“Formula 1 benefits a wide range of sectors, such as hotels, restaurants, retail and services, generating opportunities and income for the local population.

“Sao Paulo has a long-standing tradition and a historic relationship with Formula 1. Maintaining this partnership means ensuring predictability for investment, strengthening the calendar of major events and consolidating the city’s position as a global benchmark for hosting international competitions.”

Adler, CEO of Sao Paulo Grand Prix, said: “The extension of the contract of the Sao Paulo Grand Prix until 2035 is a source of immense pride, and represents recognition of work built on dedication, investment and a long-term vision.

“This renewal reaffirms Sao Paulo’s place amongst the world’s leading motorsport destinations.

“Interlagos is a unique circuit, admired by drivers, teams and fans from all over the world. It has been the setting for memorable races and is an integral part of Formula 1’s history.

“I would like to thank Domenicali and Formula 1 for their trust and partnership, as well as Mayor Nunes and Sao Paulo City Council for their extraordinary support and ongoing investment in the modernisation of Interlagos. This partnership has been fundamental to the growth and success of the event.”

title: Permane gives update on Racing Bulls driver decision process
excerpt:
Alan Permane believes that "the right decision will be made" when Racing Bulls finally confirms its 2027 driver line-up, with the team "trying to apply a little bit of science" before making any announcement.

Racing Bulls remains the only team yet to announce even one driver for next season, with both seats up for grabs and three drivers fighting for them.

Current driver Liam Lawson sits best of the rest in the drivers' standings behind the top teams, with the Kiwi sitting in P9 having also made three appearances for Red Bull this season, scoring 14 times on a Sunday.

Arvid Lindblad sits P11 in the standings, albeit 45 points behind Lawson, but has impressed in a rookie Formula 1 season that has included 11 points finishes in Grands Prix.

Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov is the third driver in contention, the Bulgarian a race winner in F2 and second in the standings during his maiden season in the junior single-seater series.

Having made his F1 debut during Free Practice 1 in Mexico, Tsolov was directly compared against Lindblad during the session, finishing just one-tenth slower.

Speaking to the media on Friday ahead of the Sao Paulo Grand Prix this weekend, Permane stated that the team were in no rush to confirm a line-up.

"Red Bull has had a very successful young driver programme," said Permane, who announced he had signed a contract extension to stay with Racing Bulls until 2031.

"And I think, and I don't want to be critical of it, but I think you guys are critical of it, [that] maybe sometimes drivers haven't been able to have enough time to settle or maybe some snap decisions have been made.

"We're trying to apply a little bit of science and that takes some time. We are looking at everything and studying, analysing and time is on our side.

"We're not in a rush to do anything and I'm very confident the right decision will be made. I realise it's frustrating for our drivers, I realise it's frustrating for everyone else, but we want to get it right and we will get it right, and I'm sure when we announce it in the coming weeks everyone will be happy."

Ahead of this weekend's race in Brazil, Lawson admitted "I don’t know what else they want me to do" having first made his F1 debut in 2023, but only completing a full campaign last season for the first time.

Permane admitted that the main area of focus would be the outright speed of a driver, but that attributes such as experience would also be an important factor in any decision.

"Main factors are, as always, pace and speed. That's what comes into it. That's the very first thing we look for but we're not just a team that exists to just solely compete," said Permane.

"We are here to bring young talent through so we have to keep an eye on that and that doesn't necessarily mean that we just keep churning young talent through the car.

"We need to have maybe some experience as well to measure that talent against. So it's not an easy decision and I understand, I get the frustration from everyone.

"I get the frustration from my drivers, however, they are both performing excellently and so I don't know if that frustration is helping, maybe they'll be even better when those decisions are made."

title: Camara reflects on 'very special' F1 weekend debut
excerpt:
Rafael Camara has reflected on a “very special” first taste of Formula 1 action with the Haas rookie making his debut at home earlier than expected.

Following confirmation earlier this week that Esteban Ocon would no longer compete for the US outfit for the rest of 2026, the 21-year-old Brazilian – who had already been signed to race for the team in 2027 – stepped up to race for Haas at this weekend’s Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

With plenty of eyes on him at his home event, Camara was positive about his first day behind the wheel – especially given it was a track he had never driven at before – as he recorded P18 and P16 finishes in FP1 and FP2 respectively.

“It’s been a very nice weekend, very special,” said Camara. “Going into FP1, it was getting a bit more emotional. You can see the crowd in front of you and everyone’s just so excited.

“Once you get in the car and start driving, you just focus on your own thing. It’s the normal thing you’ve been doing all your life.

"It’s been a very nice weekend, a lot of things going on, but so far I think it’s been a good two sessions. We’re able to learn a lot and just keep improving through the day.”

Camara also acknowledged the challenge of adapting to the current generation of F1 machinery. While he has completed TPC (Testing of Previous Car) tests with both Haas and Ferrari, today marked his first outing in a 2026 Formula 1 car.

“Once you get in the car, it’s a completely different thing,” he explained. “In a way, you get different feelings. It’s quite difficult to simulate the real car.

“There were a lot of things to learn, a lot to adapt [to], and to process. As for tomorrow, it will be good tonight to just sit back, realise everything, understand more things and put things in place for tomorrow.”

His first day of running, however, didn’t pass without incident with the Brazilian reprimanded over an impeding moment with Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc. With the Monegasque on a flying lap, he was forced to take evasive action towards the wall at Turn 15 as the inexperienced Camara moved across.

“While the typical penalty for impeding in a Free Practice session is a warning, in this instance, we are of the view that a reprimand is warranted,” read the stewards’ document as they cited the situation that had been created was “clearly dangerous”.

Asked about the incident, Haas’ Head Of Car Engineering, Hoagy Nidd explained: “He’s full throttle. He’s starting a lap. He can’t really move any further to the right in the end, but it’s just one of those things. He’s absolutely flat out at that point.”

title: Red Bull ‘looking into quite a few changes’ for Verstappen
excerpt:
Red Bull are planning to make “quite a few changes” to Max Verstappen’s car ahead of Qualifying for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix after he suffered issues with the clutch and steering during Free Practice.

Although the Dutchman finished third in both FP1 and FP2, it wasn’t the smoothest day for him as he continued to struggle with his downshifts, which has been a recurring problem this season.

He also reported heavy steering on the RB22, referring to it as a “workout”, and ultimately ended the second session slightly early because of it.

Asked whether Red Bull had resolved the steering troubles, Head of Race Strategy Hannah Schmitz responded: “I think we’ll have a different wheel for the rest of the weekend, and we’re looking into quite a few changes on Max’s side.

“There are a number of things that he was unhappy with, but we know what they all are, and they’re all things that we can work on and improve.”

Verstappen has previously explained that he relays such concerns in order to “make sure that the team is always looking into details to try and find more lap time”, which Schmitz admitted does help to unlock extra performance.

“I think there is a lot of performance to gain, and obviously, in terms of lap times, we’re still pretty competitive up there with everybody else,” she said. “So, given there’s still quite a lot of potential in the car, that looks optimistic for the rest of the weekend.

“I think it was a useful day. There’s definitely a lot of things to work on and look into overnight, but in a way, that’s what practice is for. I think there’s a lot of potential in the car, so looking forward to the rest of the weekend.”

However, she did note that the unpredictable weather at Interlagos could influence Saturday’s Qualifying hour, with rain currently forecast in the afternoon.

“It looks like it’s a very heavy rain front,” she summarised. “So whether Qualifying will actually happen at the scheduled time, I guess, is what we will find out a bit more about tomorrow.

“There are a few forecasts where it looks like it might come just after Qualifying, so there is a chance of a dry Qualifying still. We’ll be prepared for all eventualities.”

While Verstappen found himself in a tight battle with Lando Norris and George Russell in FP2 – only 0.020s separated the trio as they occupied P2 to P4 – his team mate Isack Hadjar found himself over a second adrift of the benchmark set by Kimi Antonelli.

“I was not very happy,” the Frenchman said. “I thought there was free lap time in the balance. We went in one direction and it didn't work. So, work in progress. In the end, I feel like tomorrow anyway it's going to be raining.

“But still, I want to go into FP3 and be like, okay, solved something at least. On the long run, it seems competitive.

“This morning was competitive. It's just that one-lap, single-lap pace on the soft. We need to find some easy lap time, but we know where we're heading.”

title: What the teams said – Friday in Brazil
excerpt:
What the teams said – Friday in Brazil

The drivers and teams report back from Friday practice at the Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace ahead of the Sao Paulo Grand Prix in Brazil.

Nov 06, 2026 10:35pm UTC

Mercedes

Antonelli took to the track for the first time as a World Champion in FP1, and it looked like he was happy to pick up where he left off in Mexico with a strong performance. He was up there on both the medium and soft tyres, winding up less than a tenth off the pace. He went even better in the second session, topping the timing sheet by a handsome margin. On a day where the time gaps were small, his 0.253s lead over the field was impressive.

Russell has a five-place grid drop coming for Sunday after taking on a new ICE, but ran a standard programme as he looks to try and negate that penalty as much as possible. He could not match his team mate, but was very much in the mix just behind.

Kimi Antonelli - FP1: 1:11.799, P2; FP2: 1:10.763, P1

"It was a positive day overall and I felt good in the car, particularly on the single lap runs. The conditions were quite tricky with the low grip, and it wasn’t easy to find the right balance, but I think we made some good progress between FP1 and FP2. There is still more to improve with both the car and my driving, so we’ll work through everything tonight and see what we can find for tomorrow.

"It looks very close at the front. McLaren and Red Bull look strong, and we know Ferrari can often find something extra when we get to qualifying, so I expect it to be a really tight fight. The weather could also play a part. It’s very difficult to predict at the moment, so we need to be ready for anything and react quickly if the conditions change.

"After the highs of Mexico, I’m just focusing on each session as it comes this weekend but I am enjoying things so far. Hopefully we can take another step tomorrow and put ourselves in a good position for qualifying and continue that feeling."

George Russell - FP1: 1:12.103, P5; FP2: 1:11.036, P4

"Overall, it was a solid Friday. We look to be in the mix, although it’s very close between several teams at the front. The long run pace felt stronger than our single-lap performance on my side, so there are definitely areas we can work on overnight to try and find a bit more ahead of Qualifying. The car wasn't perfect and we've got some understeer to dial out; there’s still some performance to find if we want to be fighting right at the front tomorrow.

"The conditions are likely to change across the weekend, so what we saw today won’t necessarily be fully representative of what we face tomorrow and Sunday. It looks like we’re in for another really close fight and small margins are going to make a difference.

"Obviously, the five-place grid penalty we have makes our task a little more difficult. It puts even more emphasis on having a strong qualifying and putting the car as high up the grid as possible before the penalty is applied. If we can do that, then I’m confident we can still put ourselves in a position to move forward and challenge near the front on Sunday."

Andrew Shovlin, Trackside Engineering Director

"This has been one of our better Fridays recently from a pace point of view, although there is still plenty of scope to improve the balance. FP1 was interesting as Kimi looked very comfortable on the single lap but struggled a little more on the long run, whereas George was very strong on the long run but didn’t quite get the single lap together. That gave us some useful data ahead of the afternoon and we were able to take the best elements from each set-up into FP2.

"The second session ran smoothly and, overall, we look to have decent pace on both the single lap and long run. There is still work to do though, and both drivers are finding the cars difficult in certain areas. Brake locking is one of those and has been a bit of a theme for us over the past few races. We’d also like to find a better compromise between rear grip through the high-speed corners and giving the drivers the strong front end they need in the slower sections. Whilst the pace is encouraging then, we’ve still got plenty to work on overnight. If we can make the cars a little easier for the drivers to work with and tidy up those areas of balance, hopefully we can take another step forward tomorrow."

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: Andrea Kimi Antonelli of Italy driving the (12) Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team W17 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Clive Mason/Getty Images)

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: George Russell of Great Britain driving the (63) Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team W17 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Clive Rose/Getty Images)

McLaren

Norris wound up fastest in FP1 by 0.082s from Antonelli, the McLaren man setting his lap time a few moments after the Italian and thus on a slightly more evolved track. Nonetheless it was a strong lap and showed McLaren could be in the mix here. Fornaroli also had a decent session, finishing 11th after running the soft tyre first before the track had rubbered in.

Piastri took his cockpit back in FP2, and both McLaren drivers found themselves evenly matched. Norris had the edge, but only by 0.068s.

Lando Norris - FP1: 1:11.717, P1; FP2: 1:11.016, P2

"It’s been a positive day. FP1 was a pleasant surprise, and although we found FP2 slightly more challenging compared to Mercedes, our pace relative to the rest of the field looked strong. We’ve been working through the upgrades, and the first signs are encouraging: we seem to have gained performance and a little lap time.

"The upgrades are designed to bring more load and grip, rather than alter the car’s handling, but they can still affect how the car feels. The car has been tricky this year, but today it felt a little more straightforward and positive, which is a good start to the weekend. We’ll analyse everything carefully and make sure we do our best to prepare, particularly with very wet conditions expected on Saturday."

Oscar Piastri - FP2: 1:11.084, P5

"A reasonable session to start the weekend. Everything feels good and the upgrades look positive, which is encouraging. We’ll now keep building on that to put ourselves in the best window for Qualifying tomorrow afternoon.

"There’s still a bit of work to do to catch the cars ahead, but overall, I think it was a pretty successful first day. Thanks to Leo for his efforts in FP1 and the useful work he did for the team. We’ve got plenty to look through tonight, and hopefully we can take another step forward in the remaining sessions."

Leonardo Fornaroli - FP1: 1:12.833, P11

"It was a positive FP1 session today, this was my first time at the circuit and I really enjoyed it. There was a lot to get through, particularly with the aerodynamic work at the start but I’m pleased with the progress we’ve made since Mexico. The car felt good, and I’m happy with all the work we completed today.

"Once more, thank you to the Zak, Andrea and the rest of the team for the opportunity and all their support this season. This was my final FP1 session of the year, but I’ll keep working in the simulator and supporting the team as Reserve Driver for the remaining races of the season."

Randy Singh - Senior Director, Racing

"It has been an encouraging day for the team. We brought a new upgrade package, including a revised front wing, and the data from both practice sessions indicates that it is delivering exactly as anticipated. Both drivers were immediately competitive, with Oscar doing a fantastic job to hit the pace straight away in FP2 despite sitting out the opening session in tricky, misty conditions. Leo too did a very good job in FP1, helping the team to collect very important data but also being able to show his natural speed, despite he had to run on a set of used Softs when he had the possibility to properly push for the lap time.

"The car feels like it has taken a small step forward compared to recent events, putting us in a much stronger position to compete near the front. Looking ahead to qualifying, the margins remain extremely fine across the field; a good session could easily be the difference between the front row and starting seventh or eighth. We will complete our due diligence on the data tonight before confirming our setup for the remainder of the weekend."

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: Lando Norris of Great Britain driving the (1) McLaren MCL40 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: Oscar Piastri of Australia and McLaren prepares to drive in the garage during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Hector Vivas - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: Leonardo Fornaroli of Italy and McLaren prepares to drive during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)

Red Bull

Verstappen was his usual vocal self on the radio in FP1, complaining about downshifts and also his steering wheel. Despite claiming that driving had turned into a “workout,” the Dutchman finished in the top three, a few places higher than Hadjar. He had similar issues in the second session and wound up parking in the garage earlier than planned, with the team needing to look at his steering wheel. But he was quick throughout the day, and looks right in the mix for pole. Hadjar has a little bit more work to do, he wound up down in ninth after being the first to bolt on the soft tyres.

Max Verstappen - FP1: 1:11.953, P3; FP2: 1:11.022, P3

“The session went fairly well today. We’re always looking to extract a little more performance, while also trying to find more consistency in our overall performance. We’ve been fine-tuning the car and, in particular, working to better understand the tyre behaviour over the long runs. I had some issues with the steering, which we’ll need to fix ahead of qualifying. There’s still a bit of work to do, but nothing major. We’ll focus on maximising our performance and maybe hope for a little bit of rain."

Isack Hadjar - FP1: 1:12.156, P6; FP2: 1:11.839, P9

“We had a pretty consistent day today and were competitive on the long runs this morning, although we’re still working on finding the right balance. FP2 was more challenging as we went in a different direction with the setup, which didn’t quite work out as expected. We know where we need to improve and will make some adjustments ahead of tomorrow. It looks like we could have some rain, so we’ll need to adapt to the conditions, but hopefully we can make another step forward with the car.”

Hannah Schmitz, Head of Race Strategy

“It was a useful day. There was definitely a lot of things to work on and look into, but that is what practice is for. It was a close call on which session we would run the Hard and which session we would run the Medium tyres. Ultimately most of the top teams tested the three compounds, as they are so similar, but what we will run comes down to driver and Team preference.

"For both Max and Isack, there are things they want to look into and change overnight. There is a lot of performance that we can extract, and, in terms of lap times, we are still very competitive up there with the rest of the field. The Team are looking into several changes for Max’s car. There were things he was unhappy with, but we know what they are so can work on them.

"Tomorrow, the forecast is looking wet and we will have to wait and see if Qualifying happens at the scheduled time, but we will be prepared for all eventualities.”

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: Max Verstappen of the Netherlands and Oracle Red Bull Racing prepares to drive in the garage during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Clive Rose/Getty Images)

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: Isack Hadjar of France driving the (6) Oracle Red Bull Racing RB22 Red Bull Ford Powertrains in the Pitlane during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Mark Thompson/Getty Images)

Ferrari

Beganovic was in for Leclerc in the opening session, but he did not have much chance to impress with reliability issues limiting him to just 11 laps. He did not manage to get a flying lap in on the softs, but at least Leclerc had Hamilton’s data to look through.

Hamilton had a decent first hour, but both Ferrari drivers found the second session more difficult. Neither could nail that flying lap, with Leclerc also impeded by Camara on one of his runs – something that left the Monegasque driver less than impressed on the radio.

Charles Leclerc - FP2: 1:11.483, P7

"I only drove in FP2 today and it was quite a tricky session. The feeling in the car wasn’t quite right, so there’s plenty for us to work on tonight. I have some ideas about the direction we need to take with the set-up and we’ll make some changes for tomorrow. We need to find some performance, and hopefully we can make a good step forward for qualifying."

Lewis Hamilton - FP1: 1:12.041, P4; FP2: 1:11.213, P6

"It was a challenging day. The track is very bumpy and slippery, which made it difficult to get the tyres into the right window. FP1 was okay overall, but FP2 proved more difficult. We’ve gathered plenty of useful data, so we’ll work through that with the team tonight to understand where we can improve the car ahead of qualifying tomorrow."

Dino Beganovic - FP1: 1:14.357, P21

"It was great to be back in the car and experience such an amazing track behind the wheel. The first part of the session went well, and we collected some interesting data, however, unfortunately, our session was cut short by an issue and we didn’t manage to put in as many laps as we planned.

"It’s always special to drive the SF26, and to be part of the team, and I’m thankful for the opportunity to run the car in a free practice. I hope to be back in the car soon."

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: Charles Leclerc of Monaco and Scuderia Ferrari prepares to drive in the garage during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Hector Vivas - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: Dino Beganovic of Sweden driving the (38) Scuderia Ferrari SF-26 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Buda Mendes/Getty Images)

Audi

Slater was in for Hulkenberg in the opening session, but his participation did not last long as he was forced to park up trackside with an issue. That led to a red flag stoppage, which was a shame for the rookie who was robbed of the chance to show what he is made of.

Bortoleto at least had a clean opening hour on home soil and finished in the top 10. It was much of the same for the Brazilian in FP2, as he tries to build a less incident-packed weekend than he managed last year. Hulkenberg, however, was left without a single lap on the opening day, the issue with his car preventing him from going out at all in FP2.

Nico Hulkenberg - FP2: No time set, P22

“No laps for me today. Following the issue Freddie had in FP1, the team managed to identify the problem and worked hard to fix it but, unfortunately, we ran out of time to get me out on track in FP2. I followed Gabi's session alongside the engineers, and we'll go through the data he collected. Not an easy day, but we'll try to recover and make the most of FP3 tomorrow.”

Gabriel Bortoleto - FP1: 1:12.614, P8; FP2: 1:11.780, P8

“It's been an encouraging first day overall. We had a good start to the weekend and went through all of our task-list for the day; the car felt very good out there, and that also helped me getting the most out of it. Hopefully, we can keep this energy going through the rest of the weekend.”

Freddie Slater- FP1: 1:14.966, P22

“Of course, missing a session is frustrating as a driver because you just want to drive, that's what we love to do, but I know that's part of motorsport and these things can happen. On the other hand, the laps I did were positive. On the hard tire I got some good, valuable lessons, so I’ll take that with me and move on. It's been an amazing experience over these two weekends and I am grateful to Audi Revolut F1 Team for it. I've learned so much already, both from the team and about how these cars work, and it's been a great opportunity to gain valuable experience that will help me in the future.”

SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 06: Nico Hulkenberg of Germany and Audi F1 Team looks on from the fan stage prior to practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Brazil at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace on November 06, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil. (Photo by Hector Vivas - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Alpine

Gasly sat out for Mini in FP1, and the rookie did a very good job, topping the midfield and beating his team mate. He wound up nearly a tenth ahead of Colapinto, but the Argentine still had a solid day. He was on the cusp of the top 10 in the second session, just 0.005s behind Bearman. As for Gasly, he took a little longer to get going after returning for FP2, so it remains to be seen if he can climb up the order tomorrow at a track where he has a very decent record.

Pierre Gasly - FP2: 1:12.109, P14

“A slightly different Friday to normal for me today with Gabriele [Mini] in my car for Free Practice 1, so only the one session in the car on my side during Free Practice 2. Gabriele did a great job in that session to be up in P7, and it appeared the car was quite well balanced from the very start with Franco also up inside the top 10. I do not think the leaderboard in Free Practice 2 reflects how I am feeling inside the car after that session. While I am not completely happy with a few things, it was a bit messy our end on the Soft tyre and I locked up on my first push lap and then had to abort another, so there is definitely much more performance to quickly unlock and show. I am definitely feeling optimistic, especially as a tenth of a second makes up four places or so. I have always enjoyed driving at this track, so I am looking forward to more Practice tomorrow ahead of Qualifying where we'll give it our all to be in Q3 again.”

Franco Colapinto - FP1: 1:12.654, P9; FP2: 1:11.996, P11

“It is good to be back in São Paulo and driving in Interlagos, this legendary track, always feels so special. Today went quite well and, in terms of competitiveness, we are looking quite good. We have some more work to do on the balance of the car and trying to feel more comfortable, but the team and I will work hard tonight to go through the data to see what areas we can change and improve. The underlying pace is there and the gaps to some of our rivals are very close, so it is important to maximise every detail. The track here has been resurfaced and it feels okay in the dry, some of the usual bumps remain, but, of course, we have not yet driven in wet conditions. There is some rain forecast, so that is something for us all to keep an eye on.”

Gabriele Mini - FP1: 1:12.569, P7

“I am quite happy with how my second Free Practice session with the team went and, obviously, finishing in P7 was a pretty good result. I learnt a lot of things last weekend in Mexico City, so I knew a few areas I needed to work on heading into today, which was very useful. I began the programme with some aero testing which is important for the team with the useful data it provides. After that we moved into some performance running, starting on Mediums and then onto Softs. I felt the car was in a good place and I was relatively pleased with my push lap on Softs. There was definitely more time in that lap but there is also a lot to manage inside the car, so I also know it was far from perfect. Still, I was able to show some pace which was good, I was happy with it, and it was satisfying to learn that I was amongst the quickest of everyone in some corners on the lap. It was very different to Mexico, I felt way more grip here and I was just building and improving lap after lap. Once again, thank you to the team for the opportunity and now I look forward to seeing what I can do to assist the team for the remainder of the weekend.”

(Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Haas

Camara had a solid opening session for Haas, getting plenty of laps in and setting a strong foundation for his weekend. Bearman was 12th in FP1, despite locking up his tyres early in the session.

Bearman improved on that in the second hour of practice, winding up in the top 10 which bodes well for Qualifying. Camara found the second session more testing, after drifting across onto the racing line with a flying Leclerc coming up behind. That led to a hairy moment, which the stewards had a look at after the session, giving the rookie a reprimand.

Oliver Bearman - FP1: 1:12.837, P12; FP2: 1:11.991, P10

“It was a decent day and I was happy with the car. Sometimes it was a bit more challenging than others, but we found a decent baseline. I’m proud of the guys and we’ll keep working overnight to find a bit more to see what we can do in Qualifying – not knowing what weather conditions we may be running in.”

Rafael Camara - FP1: 1:13.696, P18; FP2: 1:12.561, P16

“It’s been a really nice weekend so far, really special. Going into FP1 was getting a bit more emotional, with the intensity of the crowd in front of you and fans getting excited. Once you get into the car, and you start driving, it goes back to the normal thing that you’ve been doing your whole life. There’s a lot going on, but so far it’s been a good two sessions, learning a lot and improving throughout the day. Tonight, I’ll work with the team and put more in place for tomorrow.”

Ayao Komatsu, Team Principal

“Overall, it’s been a decent Friday. It’s the first day for our debutant Rafa in his home country, so there was a lot going on, but he and the team have handled the situation very well. He’s very calm with a professional approach, and had two solid sessions, so I’m very pleased with that and think we’ve got off to a good start. On Ollie’s side, in FP1 he wasn’t as happy with the car as he had been previously, but we’ve actually got a pretty decent reference from other races, and in FP2 he was happier, especially on the softs. We really couldn’t get the hard tyres working, so that’s something we’ve got to look into. On quali runs, because of the difference in hards and softs, we left some performance out there. I think the baseline is good, and it’s now at the fine-tuning stage of understanding what we can do better on the medium and hard compounds, and at the same time, getting a bit more out of the soft tyre.”

Racing Bulls

Lawson rounded out the top 10 in first practice in what was a steady session for him. Lindblad was further back and took avoiding action via an escape road at one point, keen not to tangle with Verstappen on track like his team mate did in Mexico. But the rookie beat Lawson in the second session, albeit on a day where the gaps were as tight in the midfield as they were up front. There was just 0.034s between the team mates in FP2, so a tight intra-team fight could be in the offing tomorrow.

Arvid Lindblad - FP1: 1:13.038, P14; FP2: 1:12.008, P12

"It’s my first time driving here at Interlagos and it’s a pretty cool track to drive, as I expected. FP1 wasn’t the smoothest session, as I still had to familiarise myself with the layout and get up to speed. In addition to this, we also identified a few areas on the car that needed improvement. We made some changes ahead of FP2, where I felt much more comfortable and confident behind the wheel, so that's a definite positive. Looking ahead to the rest of the weekend, the weather remains a bit of an unknown with rain in the forecast. The midfield is also very tight, but I believe there’s still room for us to make a step forward. We’ll keep pushing and working with the team."

Liam Lawson - FP1: 1:12.715, P10; FP2: 1:12.042, P13

"Today has been somewhat fine overall. We made some changes to the car between FP1 and FP2, but there's definitely more to be made ahead of tomorrow. We’ll spend tonight reviewing everything and working out what we need to do to get the car into the best possible window for tomorrow. We have a few ideas we’d like to explore, but the midfield is extremely close at the moment. It's going to be important to put everything together, particularly with the weather being so unpredictable."

Alan Permane, Team Principal

"It's not been our strongest Friday here in Brazil. We haven't quite got to grips with the car, but we made improvements between FP1 and FP2, so the drivers were happier. That being said, there are definitely some more adjustments to be made. We're a tiny bit out of position in comparison to where we normally are on a Friday, however we're running the simulator with ideas to find a tenth or two, and are focused on ensuring we have the best car set up ahead of tomorrow's weather forecast. We know the car runs well in the wet, so we're optimistic as we look ahead to Qualifying tomorrow."

Aston Martin

Alonso and Stroll had busy opening sessions, both completing plenty of laps. Alonso wound up near the top 10, much as he had in Mexico before it all went wrong in Qualifying. He will be hoping to avoid a repeat of last weekend, as he does seem to have taken a step towards the midfield here. As for Stroll, he had one hairy moment with Verstappen when the duo completed their practice starts at the end of FP1, but other than that had a steady day.

Fernando Alonso - FP1: 1:13.017, P13; FP2: 1:12.538, P15

Lance Stroll - FP1: 1:13.760, P19; FP2: 1:12.942, P18

Stroll said:

"It's great to be back in Brazil and I'm feeling better.

"It was good to get out on track today, we managed to get through our Friday plan and all of our running programme. We will need to look at the data now and have some work to do overnight.

"There's also a bit of uncertainty with the weather here so we'll see what the rest of the weekend brings for us."

Mike Krack, Chief Trackside Officer said:

"Our reliability seems more of a positive here in Brazil and the pace is more or less where we expected to be so far this weekend.

"The weather forecast isn't great for tomorrow and on Sunday, so let's see what we can do. We are always learning about the car and we continued that today with a relatively smooth session for both sides of the garage."

Williams

Sainz admitted after FP1 that his car is mileage limited this weekend due to running an older engine, so it was no surprise that Browning did not complete too many laps in that FW48. Albon managed a few more, but could not force his way up the leaderboard.

For the Thai driver it was much the same story in FP2, as he struggled to extract much pace from the car. Sainz wound up only a couple of places ahead, with Williams once again looking set to struggle this weekend.

Alex Albon - FP1: 1:13.511, P16; FP2: 1:12.953, P19

“We’re trying to find the middle ground with the car, and sometimes the car has felt good and other times there’s a lot of work to do. We haven't quite found the balance yet, so it's been tricky out there. We'll use the rest of the weekend as an opportunity to come up with some ideas and look at where we can improve."

Carlos Sainz - FP2: 1:12.742, P17

“Missing FP1 is never ideal, but Luke did a good job during this mileage-limited weekend. It was a tricky FP2 with low temperatures and cold tyres, so it took a bit of time to get used to that. By the end of the session, I managed to get into a rhythm and did an okay lap on the soft and a decent long run. We are experimenting with setup and doing some correlation work which will help get us in a good position for next year. The weather could bring some opportunities tomorrow.”

Luke Browning – FP1: 1:13.591, P17

“That is FP1 done and dusted here in Brazil. We had a shorter run plan today which limited our mileage but I’m looking forward to debriefing and taking the information gathered back to the team in Grove. That was my fourth and final FP1 session of the year, it’s been great to get more experience in an F1 car, and to drive this challenging track for the first time. I’m looking forward to watching Alex and Carlos for the rest of the weekend and helping the team in any way that I can.”

Cadillac

Bottas had a quiet opener for Cadillac, but it was good to see him back driving after his big crash last weekend in Mexico City. He partnered Herta, who managed a credible 31 laps in the end despite feeling unwell. In the second session, Perez just pipped his team mate by just 0.067s on a day where the gaps tended to be small. But Cadillac look set once again to prop up the field.

Valtteri Bottas - FP1: FP2: 1:13.371, P15; FP2: 1:13.383, P21

“FP1 went well and the pace was encouraging, while in FP2 we focused more on the long runs and understanding the car over a longer stint. Interlagos is always a great track to drive, so it’s been good to get back out there. We’ll dive into the data tonight to see where we can find some more performance and put ourselves in the best possible position for qualifying tomorrow.”

Sergio Perez - FP1: 1:13.316, P20

“Good first session for me. The changing weather conditions could definitely create opportunities for us this weekend. We haven’t made a final decision yet on whether we’ll take an additional engine and therefore a penalty, so that’s something we’ll discuss tonight before deciding on our approach for the rest of the weekend. We know anything can happen, particularly in these conditions, and we’ll be ready to make the most of any opportunities that come our way.”

Colton Herta – FP1: 1:14.275, P20

“All wrapped up here in Brazil with Free Practice 1 and what a fantastic track. It’s my first time driving here and it’s been a lot of fun. It’s always a privilege to drive the car, and to be able to do it in three consecutive weekends was amazing. I hope the data can help Checo and Valtteri as we build throughout the weekend.”

Marcin Budkowski, Team Principal

“It’s been a relatively smooth day of running today. Colton had a solid session in FP1 on his track debut here, completing good mileage and gathering valuable data and feedback for the team. In FP2, both Checo and Valtteri completed their run plans and we’ll consolidate their feedback as we plan for qualifying. Operationally, our objective is to maximise every session to prepare ourselves for an unpredictable weekend ahead. With changeable weather conditions often a factor at Interlagos, strong execution will be key to taking advantage of whatever comes our way.”

(Photo by Hector Vivas - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Pirelli

Simone Berra, Pirelli Chief Engineer

“The two free practice sessions were held in very different conditions, providing teams with valuable information ahead of the next two days. In FP1, the higher temperatures led to increased thermal degradation and greater tyre sliding, particularly on the C3. As a result, much of the race simulation work was carried out on the C4 and C5, often with little tyre management, as teams sought to explore their operating limits. Even in these conditions, all three compounds came up to performance quickly from the opening laps, with no significant warm-up issues.

"The second session took place in considerably cooler temperatures and under changeable weather conditions. Some teams experienced greater difficulty bringing the front tyres up to temperature during qualifying simulations, while long-run performance appeared more favourable thanks to reduced overheating and lower degradation levels. The Soft delivered particularly consistent behaviour and confirmed a strong level of performance.

"The absence of graining and similar abrasion levels across all three compounds suggest that degradation will continue to be driven primarily by thermal effects, with wear on the rear-right tyre becoming a factor over longer stints. With forecasts indicating even cooler temperatures for Sunday and a greater than 60% chance of rain, all options remain open at this stage, including wet-weather scenarios. In dry conditions, a two-stop strategy also appears viable, given the relative ease of overtaking at Interlagos. We will continue to analyse the data from the upcoming sessions before reaching any definitive conclusions.”

title: Ferrari have 'plenty to work on' in Brazil – Leclerc
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc believes Ferrari have "plenty to work on" as the team try to find performance after Friday practice ahead of the Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

Having shown strong pace in Mexico last weekend as Lewis Hamilton took pole position and finished second with Leclerc fourth, the Scuderia appears to lack the outright speed of Mercedes and McLaren in Brazil.

Having missed Free Practice 1 in place of rookie driver Dino Beganovic, Leclerc was back behind the wheel in FP2 and finished P7, seven tenths adrift of Kimi Antonelli's top time.

"FP2 was very tricky actually, if anything one of the worst feelings I've had this year in the car," said Leclerc.

"There's plenty to work on and it didn't feel quite right but I've got some ideas. We'll change the car I think quite significantly and we'll see how it goes.

"I hope we can do a step forward because even though I missed FP1, I don't think there was much performance in that. It's just the raw pace wasn't great today."

Ferrari entered the weekend under a cloud as Leclerc and Hamilton's intra-team battle in Mexico was a talking point in the paddock, the pair only speaking about the incident after meeting in Brazil.

While Team Principal Fred Vasseur made his feelings clear on Friday, Leclerc stated that the air had been cleared and the matter settled.

He said: "We've spoken, I think everything is settled and I'm looking forward for the rest of the weekend now."

The talks had not taken place earlier as Leclerc had to rush back home to Monaco, with his wife giving birth to their first child during the week, meaning Leclerc arrived late in Brazil.

"It's definitely the most special thing ever," he reflected on the birth of his daughter. "You kind of expect it because I've always wanted to be a young dad, and with Alex we obviously felt it was the right time.

"It's a very, very special moment and definitely a week I'll forever remember for all the positive reasons. Of course, there's been other things going on as well but for me this week was all about Bianca, and it's been incredible."

title: Breaking: Lewis Hamilton, Charles Leclerc and Max Verstappen grid penalties confirmed
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen both know exactly how to bounce back from São Paulo grid penalties!

The FIA has confirmed that Lewis Hamilton, Charles Leclerc and Max Verstappen will all serve a grid penalty in the São Paulo Grand Prix.

Hamilton and Leclerc both endured a difficult opening day in Interlagos with the Scuderia once again struggling at high-speed, with the decision being taken to fit a new engine outside their allocated pools.

The seven-time world champion and Leclerc have both received a 10-place grid penalty after taking a new internal combustion engine, the first of that component outside their legal pools.

Friday was also challenging for Verstappen, with Red Bull deciding to perform several power unit component changes. As a result, the Dutchman will likely start from the last row of the grid.

Verstappen has taken a new internal combustion engine, turbocharger and exhaust set, resulting in a 30-place grid penalty. Each component is the first outside the allocated pool.

Hamilton, Leclerc and Verstappen are not the only drivers affected this weekend.

George Russell will also drop five places after Mercedes fitted an additional internal combustion engine outside his allocation, following a mechanical failure that forced the team into a larger power unit change at the Singapore Grand Prix earlier in the season.

Cadillac's Sergio Perez has also received a 30-place grid penalty after taking a new internal combustion engine, turbocharger and MGU-K.

Lewis Hamilton needing 2021 repeat; Max Verstappen 2024 wet masterclass

It would not be the first time Hamilton or Verstappen has turned a grid penalty at this circuit into a triumph.

Back in 2021, when he was still driving for Mercedes, Hamilton was handed a five-place grid drop in Brazil after the team installed a fifth internal combustion engine of that season, exceeding his allocation.

Mercedes had made the change due to concerns over power degradation and reliability issues linked to earlier power unit batches.

Hamilton was further demoted to the back of the Sprint grid that weekend after being disqualified from qualifying, with stewards ruling that the gap between his rear wing's DRS elements had exceeded the permitted 85-millimetre limit, a defect attributed to mechanical damage rather than deliberate rule-breaking.

Despite starting that race down in tenth, Hamilton produced a dominant drive through the field at Interlagos to take victory ahead of Max Verstappen, underlining just how much overtaking opportunity the circuit can offer even from a compromised grid slot.

Verstappen produced one of the great recovery drives of his career at the venue in 2024, storming from 17th on the grid in treacherous, rain-affected conditions to win going away, setting the fastest lap along the way as he beat Esteban Ocon by nearly 20 seconds.

Pierre Gasly completed an Alpine one-two in third, while Hamilton could only salvage 10th from 14th on the grid that day.

title: Breaking: Legendary fan favourite F1 grand prix handed contract extension
excerpt:
The São Paulo Grand Prix has had its contract extended until the 2035 season, Formula 1 has officially confirmed.

Interlagos is one of the most popular stops on the calendar among fans and drivers. The circuit near São Paulo has a long history of producing drama, helped in no small part by its famously unpredictable weather.

Over the years it has hosted numerous iconic races, including several memorable wet-weather drives.

Max Verstappen famously rose from starting at the back of the grid to win in treacherous conditions in 2023, while Lewis Hamilton won from 10th in 2021.

The 2008 edition also remains etched in the sport's history, when Lewis Hamilton passed Timo Glock through the final corner complex on the last lap to seal his maiden world title.

Interlagos was already contracted to host the race through to 2030. Formula 1 has now extended that deal further, meaning the São Paulo is set to remain on the calendar for five more years beyond that date.

Stefano Domenicali, President and CEO of F1, said: "Brazil is an important part of Formula 1’s history and our future, and I am delighted that this five-year extension will see us continue racing in São Paulo until 2035.

"The passion of our Brazilian fans is extraordinary, and every time we return to Interlagos we feel their energy in the grandstands and in the city of São Paulo. Brazil has produced an incredible 33 Formula 1 drivers, including Gabriel Bortoleto and Rafael Câmara who are racing this weekend in front of their home crowd, which will add to the many previous unforgettable racing moments in São Paulo.

"The continued success and excitement surrounding the event shows why it holds such a special place on our calendar, and this agreement underlines our long-term commitment to Brazil. I would like to thank the Mayor of São Paulo, Ricardo Nunes, and the President and CEO of São Paulo Grand Prix, Alan Adler, for their continued commitment and investment.

"Together, we will build on this success and make the experience even better for our fans in the years ahead."

title: Mercedes facing unexpected problem after powerful Sao Paulo GP start
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli made a perfect start to life as world champion in Interlagos by topping FP2.

Mercedes has admitted both George Russell and Kimi Antonelli are battling understeer for the first time since the team's major upgrade package landed in Malaysia, despite Antonelli topping Friday's second practice session at Interlagos.

The Italian set the pace with a 1:10.763, edging out Lando Norris and Max Verstappen, with Russell fourth fastest as Mercedes continued to look competitive on Friday.

But Mercedes' deputy team principal Bradley Lord struck a cautious tone when discussing the car's underlying balance, pointing to a handling trait the squad had not seen since introducing its seven-part aerodynamic update at Sepang.

Speaking after FP2, Lord said the Silver Arrows look in the fight but that understeer needs dialling out for both drivers.

"Real progress is hitting the ground running with the car," said Lord. "Both drivers are still looking to dial out some understeer, which is not something we've had too much of since we put the update package on in Malaysia.

"So, overall, long-run pace looks in the mix with Lando [Norris], Max [Verstappen] and both of our guys. So maybe Ferrari are half a step behind, but I'm sure they'll come good as well in the hotter conditions."

Has Mercedes finally understood Malaysia upgrades?

Conditions at Interlagos on Friday turned changeable, with air temperatures dropping below 20 degrees Celsius during FP2 and light drizzle disrupting tyre warm-up.

Saturday is forecast to be considerably warmer, before temperatures fall again on race day, a swing Lord suggested would offer a genuine test of how well Mercedes understands its new aerodynamic package across varying track conditions.

Asked whether the operating window of the upgrade is becoming better understood within the team, Lord was candid about the uncertainty that remains.

"That's a good question," said Lord. "I'm not quite sure how we would answer that, to be honest. We'll see.

"This weekend we've got a great test of it, with cool conditions [on Friday], much warmer on Saturday and then cool again on Sunday, and whether we can cope with that sort of adjustment in track temperature and what it does to the balance as well."

title: Lewis Hamilton set for Sao Paulo GP grid penalty after difficult start
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton is set to take a grid penalty at Interlagos this weekend after Ferrari opted for a fresh engine element beyond his season allocation, RacingNews365 understands.

Under FIA sporting regulations, exceeding the permitted number of power unit components triggers a 10-place grid penalty for the first additional element introduced, dropping to five places for any further changes beyond that point.

It remains unclear exactly where Hamilton will be demoted to on the grid once qualifying is completed and whether it is a full engine change.

The timing is notable given the parallel with 2021, when Hamilton took a five-place penalty for fitting a fifth Mercedes engine of that season ahead of the same event.

Starting 10th that day, Hamilton produced one of the defining drives of his career, working through a two-stop strategy on medium and then hard tyres to hunt down and pass Max Verstappen for the win.

Interlagos lends itself to recovery drives of that nature. The long uphill run from Junção through Arquibancadas feeds a slipstreaming blast into the Senna S, setting up a counter-attack opportunity moments later into Turn 4.

The compact 4.309km lap keeps the field tightly bunched across all 71 laps, while heavy tyre degradation through the circuit's high-load corners regularly produces pace deltas that reward cars running fresher rubber.

Changeable weather at the São Paulo venue has historically added another layer of unpredictability, increasing both driver error and the scope for late-race passing moves.

Hamilton arrives at the circuit third in the drivers' championship on 259 points, just two behind Verstappen, with Ferrari needing a repeat of that 2021 charge.

title: McLaren relief as Brazil upgrades offer Lando Norris-Oscar Piastri boost
excerpt:
McLaren's sporting director Randy Singh has given an encouraging early verdict on the team's new upgrade package after the first day of running at Interlagos.

The Woking-based squad brought a wide-ranging aerodynamic update to the São Paulo Grand Prix, covering the front wing, rear wing, beam wing and floor furniture, as it looks to arrest a recent dip in form against Red Bull, Ferrari and Mercedes.

The changes follow updates introduced in Baku and Austin that failed to deliver the expected gains.

Lando Norris topped first practice before Kimi Antonelli went fastest in second practice, with Norris second and Oscar Piastri fifth as the team worked through its new parts across both sessions.

Reserve driver Leonardo Fornaroli was drafted in for FP1 to help evaluate the new specification in detail, with it being Piastri's turn to watch from the pit wall.

Asked if McLaren was pleased with the introduction of the upgrades, Singh said it had gone well.

"No, it went really well," said Singh. "I think the upgrades look like they're delivering as we expected, which is all you can ask for.

"And Leo [Fornaroli] did a good job for us in FP1, running some rakes and helping us test them in detail. So yeah, from that side of things, very well."

McLaren enjoy strongest day for several grands prix

Singh also reported that Norris and Piastri had both come away happy with the car's behaviour, despite tricky conditions through the Friday running.

"Yeah, I think both drivers [are happier]," added Singh. "I'd say Oscar, having missed FP1, he's done really well, like immediately on the pace, which is not easy when you miss the first session.

"And with the slightly drizzly, misty conditions that we had, both drivers were competitive. I think hopefully the upgrades have moved us a small step forward compared to recent events, but it just remains always so tight.

"We're going to have to make sure we optimise qualifying to get a good result."

title: Max Verstappen urges Red Bull problem fix as wet weather plea issued
excerpt:
Max Verstappen ended second practice for the São Paulo Grand Prix third fastest but flagged a steering problem that Red Bull will need to resolve before qualifying. He also hopes for the arrival of wet weather.

The Dutchman set a best lap of 1m 11.022 at Interlagos, finishing just 0.006s off George Russell's Mercedes and 0.259s behind session pacesetter Kimi Antonelli. Lando Norris split the two Mercedes in second for McLaren.

But the lap times told only part of the story. Verstappen had already reported heavy steering feel during the opening session on Friday, a problem that compromised the car's rotation through the lap, and the issue was still on his mind after FP2.

"The session went fairly well," said Verstappen. "We're always looking to extract a little more performance, while also trying to find more consistency in our overall performance.

"We've been fine-tuning the car and, in particular, working to better understand the tyre behaviour over the long runs. I had some issues with the steering, which we'll need to fix ahead of qualifying. There's still a bit of work to do, but nothing major.

"We'll focus on maximising our performance and maybe hope for a little bit of rain."

The forecast appears to back him up. Saturday's qualifying session faces an estimated 50 to 70 percent chance of rain, with the potential for afternoon thunderstorms, while Sunday's race is expected to be cooler with precipitation odds between 40 and 60 percent through the afternoon.

Whether the steering complaint stems from hydraulic assistance degradation or a mechanical front-geometry issue remains unclear, leaving Red Bull with a diagnostic puzzle to solve before Verstappen heads out for a session he may be quietly hoping gets rained on.

title: Lewis Hamilton career highs and heartbreak revisited ahead of staggering milestone
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton is set to hit a major career milestone this weekend, one which only Fernando Alonso has achieved.

7 November 11:30AM

Lewis Hamilton will make the 400th Grand Prix start of his career this weekend at Interlagos, a milestone no other driver in Formula 1 history has reached without leaving the sport for a period.

The Ferrari driver, now 41, made his debut with McLaren back in 2007 and has gone on to collect 106 wins, 209 podiums and 105 pole positions across 20 seasons, seven of which ended with him as world champion.

What sets Hamilton's longevity apart is not simply the number of races but the fact he has kept winning across three separate decades, a distinction that marks him out even from Fernando Alonso, whose own record-breaking start count, now at 444 races, has included stretches away from front-running machinery and F1 entirely.

RacingNews365 takes a deeper look at Hamilton's F1 highs but also the lows...

Driver

Lewis Hamilton

British

The highs: Turkey, Silverstone and a Brazilian stampede

Among the 106 victories, two are consistently singled out by analysts as Hamilton's finest. His win at the 2008 British Grand Prix is regarded as a wet-weather masterclass, with the then-McLaren driver navigating treacherous conditions at Silverstone without error while lapping the majority of the field.

12 years later, his victory at the 2020 Turkish Grand Prix delivered a seventh world title to match Michael Schumacher's record, achieved by nursing a single set of intermediate tyres on a newly resurfaced, low-grip Istanbul Park surface that caught out much of the grid.

The 2008 season finale at Interlagos, the very circuit hosting this weekend's round, also features prominently in assessments of his career-defining moments. Late rain forced a decisive tyre call and a final-corner pass on the last lap that settled the drivers' championship in Hamilton's favour.

The same venue produced another standout performance in 2021. Hamilton arrived in São Paulo having been disqualified from Friday qualifying after his Mercedes failed a DRS aperture check, demoting him to the back for the sprint, and then took a separate five-place grid penalty for a fresh engine, leaving him down in 10th for the grand prix itself.

He fought from 20th to fifth in the sprint before converting his lowly starting slot of 10th into a staggering victory on Sunday, surviving a tense wheel-to-wheel battle with Max Verstappen along the way, a drive widely held up as one of the great recovery performances of his career.

Not every statistic-laden win is viewed equally by pundits, however. Some of his lights-to-flag victories during Mercedes' hybrid-era dominance are regarded by commentators as less revealing of raw racecraft, given the scale of the car's advantage at the time.

Races such as the 2018 German Grand Prix and the 2014 Bahrain Grand Prix are instead held up as underrated examples of Hamilton's ability, the former a recovery from a lowly grid slot in mixed conditions, the latter a battle against Nico Rosberg enjoying a clear strategic tyre advantage.

Article continues below the image...

© xpb.cc

The lows: heartbreak, controversy and barren spells

Hamilton's record is not without its darker chapters. The most painful of all came at the 2021 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, where he crossed the line second to Verstappen after race director Michael Masi allowed only the five lapped cars between the two title rivals to unlap themselves before immediately calling in the safety car for a one-lap shootout finish.

The decision cost Hamilton what would have been a record eighth world championship and triggered a lengthy FIA inquiry, which concluded that the handling of lapped traffic had been down to human error, while also finding that Masi had acted in good faith despite intense pressure from competing teams.

The fallout saw Masi removed from his post as race director ahead of the following season, direct radio communication between team principals and race control banned, an off-site virtual race control centre introduced, and the sporting regulations rewritten so that "all cars" rather than "any cars" must be permitted to pass the safety car.

Other setbacks have shaped his career in less dramatic but still significant ways. In 2007, a title that looked within reach slipped away at the Chinese Grand Prix when McLaren left him out too long on worn intermediate tyres in drying conditions, before Hamilton made a crucial mistake himself by driving into the pit-entry gravel trap.

Two years later, the 2009 Australian Grand Prix "Liegate" affair saw Hamilton disqualified after he and McLaren misled stewards over whether he had deliberately yielded position to Jarno Trulli under the safety car, a controversy that dented his reputation at the time.

The 2011 season is often cited as his most difficult on-track campaign, defined by a string of collisions, notably with Felipe Massa, and frequent trips to see the stewards.

In 2016, mechanical unreliability derailed his title bid, an engine failure while leading the Malaysian Grand Prix handing a decisive swing in the championship to teammate Rosberg.

More recently, the introduction of the 2022 ground-effect regulations brought an extended competitive drought, as Mercedes' porpoising-afflicted early chassis left Hamilton grappling with handling problems far removed from his accustomed front-running form.

Quite where this weekend's race in Brazil, the scene of one of his most dramatic triumphs, will rank among those 400 starts remains to be seen.

title: Oliver Bearman opens up on 'really missing' Esteban Ocon at Haas
excerpt:
The fallout continues from Esteban Ocon's exit from Haas.

Oliver Bearman has conceded to "really missing" Esteban Ocon at Haas, after the Frenchman was dropped by the team for the remainder of the 2026 season following an internal dispute in Mexico City.

Haas confirmed earlier this week that Ocon would not drive for the team again this year after a Friday evening fallout in Mexico. The American outfit has declined to elaborate on what happened behind closed doors.

Japanese driver Ryo Hirakawa stepped into the cockpit at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, whilst Rafael Camara, who replaces Ocon for next season, will make his debut for Haas this weekend on home soil in São Paulo. Hirakawa is unavailable due to a clash with his World Endurance Championship commitments with Toyota at Monza.

Speaking to media including RacingNews365, Bearman said the situation had left a mark on the garage.

"It's strange not having Esteban here, and it's obviously a challenging situation for everybody," said Bearman. "And I really, really feel for him. I really do feel for him.

"Of course, the situation is complicated, things have changed, and I just hope that it doesn't cause disruption. At least last week, I wouldn't say that it caused any disruption at all.

"If anything, the positive now is that we have Rafa in the car for these events, and that is also preparing us as a team for next year."

[Article continues below]

With Camara set to be Bearman's full-time partner from 2027 regardless, the Briton suggested the early switch had its upside.

"I'm excited to have a teammate who is going to push me really hard, and of course, I've had that across the years," said Bearman.

"Esteban pushed me hard, but Rafa is also going to be a very strong competitor, and for us as competitive people, as racing drivers, you want someone who pushes you to the next level, and that's the best way to get the most out of the team, for sure."

Bearman and Camara go back further than their current paddock status suggests, both having come through the Ferrari Driver Academy together.

"We joined the Academy at the same time," said Bearman. "When I first came to Italy for my first kind of scouting camp, Rafa was there as well. I remember he was very shy, and didn't speak much English. He's still pretty shy, but he speaks a lot more English now, which is good.

"But I've always had a good relationship with him. He's a funny guy and a very nice guy as well.

"To be honest, we never raced in the same category because I was always one step ahead just because of how things worked out.

"But we spent a lot of time together, a lot of training camps, a lot of fitness tests, a lot of horrible things that we don't look back on with much happiness. But we know each other well and have a good relationship."

title: Danial Ricciardo contact confirmed over possible Formula E switch
excerpt:
Fortescue Zero Racing has confirmed that contact was made with Daniel Ricciardo, though the Australian gave no indication he is ready to return to competitive racing.

The admission came from team principal Jim Wright and Fortescue founder Dr Andrew Forrest at the outfit's official launch in London on Friday evening, where Fortescue Zero Racing unveiled its black and neon green livery as the first Australian-owned team in Formula E.

Fortescue acquired Penske Autosport in September to form the new entry, which will run customer Jaguar Gen4 powertrains from the 2026-27 season.

Ricciardo has not raced since his final Formula 1 start at the 2024 Singapore Grand Prix, with Racing Bulls cutting ties that September. He confirmed his full retirement from motor racing a year later, in September 2025, as he took up an ambassadorial role with Ford.

Formula E Notebook had reported that an approach was made, with Wright confirming there was nothing more.

"I certainly didn't have any talks, but I think there was a reach-out to him, and I think the message came back: look, he's not contemplating reviving his racing career at the moment," Wright told RacingNews365 during an interview.

"He's busy doing lots of other things, which he seems to be enjoying, so I don't think we ever wanted to be in a position where we're trying to convince someone to drive. But yeah, great driver, and if he ever comes back to racing, you know, we definitely have a conversation."

Asked the same question during a roundtable including RacingNews365, Forrest downplayed any formal approach.

"Look, I think of Ricciardo more as an Aussie mate," he said. "I haven't reached out to him apart from on the way here.

"I said, 'Oh my God, Daniel Ricciardo!' Give him a yell and just tell him what we're doing. But that's it. That's been my only reach-out. But that's as a mate."

Fortescue might not have one Dan, but it does have another

While Fortescue does not have Ricciardo, it does have another former Red Bull driver in Dan Ticktum who was part of the Austrian outfit's junior programme.

Ticktum joins from Cupra Kiro, with Forrest a real fan of what the British driver brings to the new outfit.

"Look, I'm delighted to be the first Australian-owned team in Formula E," added Forrest. "However, we've got another Dan, Dan Ticktum, who I reckon is a little weapon.

"He's got the humility, he's got the drive, he's had a few scrapes. He's very, very talented. He's clocked up, I think, the fifth-fastest time in the world at Goodwood. So, look, instead of looking over the horizon, I want to back the people that we have."

The second seat remains unresolved. Taylor Barnard, announced in October as the team's other signing, boycotted the London launch amid a legal dispute initiated by his management to void his contract so he can pursue a move to Fusion Formula E.

Fortescue maintains Barnard remains legally bound to the team, with FIA Formula E's general provisions requiring the squad's consent for any transfer between nominated entries.

title: George Russell 'praying' Mercedes issues end as post-Mexico investigation launched
excerpt:
George Russell has explained how he is "praying" that the bad luck which has destroyed his season ends soon, as he revealed the outcome of an investigation.

Russell's faint title hopes finally came to an end in Mexico City, where Kimi Antonelli claimed the crown - but the Briton suffered yet another issue at the start of the race.

From second on the grid, a deployment issue on the run to Turn 1 limited his top-speed as he fell to sixth - and then was swamped by others and could not make forward progress.

He also earned a 10-second time penalty for colliding with Isack Hadjar, before quickly leaving the circuit and not being a part of the post-race celebrations.

Looking ahead to the Sao Paulo GP weekend, Russell, who finished fifth and fourth in the two Friday practice sessions, declared that he had no expectations for the weekend, but was "praying" the issues outside of his control would soon end.

"Do I come in with high expectations? Honestly, no, to be honest, but I’m looking forward to next year for sure, and we’ll just continue to work on the things that I can control, and pray the things outside of my control sort themselves out," Russell told media, including RacingNews365.

Turning to the few days between Mexico and Brazil, Russell revealed that he had a deep-dive with his engineering team, as they found that they had only had six trouble-free weekends all season.

“Post-Mexico, I was just more disappointed with how the race unfolded," he said.

"It felt like a good opportunity to fight for the victory. Starting P2 in Mexico is always a great chance to go for the lead at Turn 1, and then just another race with something outside of your control [happening] was very difficult to accept.

"I went through every race this season with my engineers, and we’ve only had six races this season where we had no issue.

"So, in 14 of those races we’ve had things that have been what we thought was bad luck, but we need to start questioning things more deeply when it’s happening so often, and especially on our side, so that was the main feeling for me."

title: Toto Wolff offers ‘as simple as that’ solution to Middle East F1 travel dilemma
excerpt:
Toto Wolff has delivered a "as simple as that" message to members of the MotoGP and F1 paddocks who do not want to travel to the Middle East.

MotoGP is racing in Qatar this weekend, with major uncertainty still in the region with the Iran War, despite most riders said to be against taking part, and the Yamaha factory team withdrawing completely from the event.

F1 is not due in Qatar until the weekend of November 28th-30th, with the season set to conclude in Abu Dhabi on December 6th, with F1 insisting that both races will go ahead, following the official travel advice of the United Kingdom Foreign, Commonwealth, and Development Office (FCDO).

This currently does not advise against travel to the region, only informing those who do to take precautions and have alternative travel arrangements in place.

Offering his latest take on the situation, Wolff declared that if somebody did not want to drive or ride in the Middle East, they simply shouldn't go.

"Stefano [Domenicali] and Mohammed [ben Sulayem] have been pretty clear about the situation: Formula 1 follows the international guidelines," Wolff began to media, including RacingNews365.

"That is travel restrictions, airlines not flying, any warnings in the region, the kind of feedback that local governments are making, so not only the promoters, but what the local governments are making, and this is what you need to rely on in my opinion, and I'm fully with that.

"I think that if [MotoGP] riders stand up, that geopolitically knows nothing about what's going on, but have the audience that listens, I think that is something that creates media value, but I would have done the same that MotoGP management has done.

"'Do you want to ride or drive?' If you don't want to, don't go.' It is as simple as that, and everybody can make their personal decisions on that, and I respect that.

"Of course, you've got to be wary of what's happening in the next few days and few weeks, and Stefano has his finger on the pulse to monitor that.

"If things were to get more dangerous, and we would get that feedback, then he's going to be the first one, together with Mohammed, to protect the people who were meant to travel, and so that's why I'm following their guidance on what I'm hearing."

[Article continues below]

Internally at Mercedes

The Austrian then went on to talk about the internal dynamics around the situation at Mercedes - where he indicated he would not hold any grudges against any team member who did not want to travel.

"Internally, it hasn't been raised. It hasn't been a topic, but if someone feels he doesn't feel comfortable, he or she doesn't feel comfortable in travelling, then it's something that I would always respect, and maybe that's an opportunity to give somebody else a chance," Wolff said.

"It wouldn't change anything for the relationship. I've always respected that, that some people don't want to go to certain grands prix, and that's how I see it at the moment."

title: Charles Leclerc releases 'frustration' in Ferrari meeting after 'crazy week'
