It seems it was good to clear the air, according to Charles Leclerc

Charles Leclerc believes airing "frustration" in a Ferrari meeting with team principal Fred Vasseur and team-mate Lewis Hamilton was "needed" at the end of what had been "a crazy week" for the Monégasque.

Thursday's meeting in São Paulo between the trio ahead of this weekend's grand prix at Interlagos was used to clear the air after the pair's on-track incident in Mexico City on Sunday.

The two Ferrari drivers made contact at Turn 4 on the opening lap of the Mexico City Grand Prix, running wide together before Leclerc rejoined ahead of his team-mate across the grass. It was the latest flashpoint between the two this year, after a similar first-lap dispute at Monza in September.

Leclerc took responsibility for the Monza collision and sat down with Hamilton to resolve it at the time. But the Mexico clash reopened old wounds, leading Hamilton to claim there were "big problems", and prompting Ferrari to schedule fresh internal talks.

Leclerc, who became a father for the first time in the days after the Mexico race, said the timing had made it difficult to address the matter sooner.

Speaking about Thursday's meeting, Leclerc said it was productive.

"It was really good to discuss all together," he said, speaking to media, including RacingNews365, following Friday practice.

"Obviously, for me, it's been a bit of a crazy week, and positively because I became a father for the first time, so we didn't necessarily have time to discuss.

"I think discussing whatever is left, or whatever frustration is left, was needed. Now I feel it's fully settled, and I don't think we should be speaking about it too much going forward."

Leclerc - 'One of the worst Friday feelings'

While the atmosphere between the drivers appeared settled, Ferrari's Friday running in Brazil brought a fresh set of problems, with Hamilton finishing practice sixth and Leclerc seventh, and with both reporting a car that felt badly out of balance.

Leclerc did not hide his frustration with the SF-26's performance after FP2.

"It's been a very, very difficult Friday," he said. "The feeling was very poor inside the car, so we've got a lot of work to do, and probably more than other weekends; we need to change the car quite a lot from today to tomorrow. It just felt quite strange in a way, so lots of changes need to be made."

Asked where the problems lay, Leclerc explained that the issues went beyond Ferrari's known straight-line deficit against rivals such as Mercedes.

"We were losing in the straights, but I think the car in the corners just felt...probably one of the worst Friday feelings of the season," he remarked.

"So I think there's a lot to be found in the corners, more than on the straights, where we know we have a deficit, but normally we are very fast in the corners, and this was not the case."

Leclerc said he had identified potential fixes but was not certain they would be sufficient to turn things around before qualifying.

"I've got quite a lot of ideas on what to change, and I think there will be significant changes going into tomorrow," he said.

"Whether that will be enough [because] the issues we had were quite big, but there's no reason why we should struggle so much more on a track like this, so we need to find a solution."

title: Red Bull reveal cause behind premature Max Verstappen Brazil practice stoppage
excerpt:
Max Verstappen was spotted jumping out of his Red Bull car with several minutes remaining in the second practice session.

Red Bull has detailed why Max Verstappen did not complete his long run programme at the end of free practice two on Saturday in Brazil.

Verstappen was spotted jumping out of the car with several minutes still remaining on the clock, while rival teams continued to circle and gather data ahead of Sunday's grand prix.

The four-time champion set the third-fastest lap in the qualifying simulations, behind Kimi Antonelli and Lando Norris.

However, Verstappen found his car much more challenging to drive when it came to the high-fuel runs, resulting in Red Bull pulling the plug early to carry out changes before Saturday's on-track action.

"It was just finding a lot of inconsistency in the long run, and we didn't feel like it was helpful anymore.

"We weren't getting the data we needed.

"We knew the things that we wanted to be looking at and changing overnight, so we just went straight into that."

Red Bull highlight 'good thing' about driver complaints

Both Verstappen and team-mate Isack Hadjar were heard complaining about the car during practice, with Verstappen's complaints primarily directed towards his steering.

While the comments highlighted areas of weakness within the RB22, Schmitz stated it is a positive development for Red Bull as it helps understand where improvements can be made.

"Everyone agrees that there's a lot of potential within the car," Schmitz said.

"Both drivers, there are things that they want to look into and change overnight, but in a way, that's a good thing.

"That means we know what's happening on the car and what we can address, and there is a lot of potential and optimism for the rest of the weekend."
